name: PDO nose thread lift

lead: A PDO nose thread lift is a minimally invasive, non-surgical rhinoplasty in which absorbable polydioxanone threads are inserted under the skin of the nose, sometimes together with filler, to raise the bridge or tip. People use it for a temporary reshaping with the lift visible soon after treatment.
Published literature is sparse: a 2024 review of clinical cases in Skin Research and Technology and one small registered trial of 10 people.

paras: Absorbable threads are placed under the skin to add support and volume, and the result lasts only as long as the threads take to absorb. It is promoted as an alternative to surgery for people who want a reversible change.
A 2024 review discusses adverse effects of nose thread procedures and prevention methods. The result is temporary as the threads absorb. It is performed by trained clinicians.

web.title: Non-surgical rhinoplasty through minimal invasive nose thread procedures (full text, PMC)

angle.text: PDO thread lifts are promoted as a non-surgical way to raise the nasal bridge or tip, sometimes combined with filler, with the lift visible soon after treatment. Absorbable threads under the skin add support, and the result is temporary as they absorb. Published evidence is limited to a case-based review and a small trial.

lead: A PDO nose thread lift is a minimally invasive, non-surgical rhinoplasty procedure in which absorbable polydioxanone (PDO) threads are inserted under the skin of the nose, sometimes together with filler, to raise the bridge or lift the tip. People choose it for a straighter, higher-looking bridge or a more defined tip without an operation.[1]

A 2024 review in Skin Research and Technology describes using absorbable 'volumizing' threads, mostly PDO and often barbed, with fillers: longer threads support the bridge and shorter ones lift the tip. Because the threads supply structural support, the authors say less filler is needed, which lowers the risk of an overly wide nose, and the combination allows more precise contouring than filler alone.[1][2]

The published literature is small: the 2024 case-based review and one registered pilot trial of 10 participants.[1][3] The related thread-lift technique for facial sagging is described as working by prompting collagen production as the threads dissolve over about six months.[4]
infobox: About six months, two to three times (authors' experience)

paras: A 2024 review describes non-surgical rhinoplasty using absorbable 'volumizing threads' combined with fillers, and explores whether this gives more precise nasal contouring than filler alone.[1] Longer threads are used along the bridge and shorter ones for tip lift; the authors say the technique may last longer than filler alone.[2]

Non-surgical rhinoplasty more generally uses injectable fillers, usually hyaluronic acid or calcium hydroxyapatite, to raise a flat bridge, lift a drooping tip or smooth bumps. Wikipedia notes that because fillers add volume they cannot reduce nose size, although a straighter-looking nose can appear smaller.[5]

PDO threads provide mechanical support under the skin and are absorbed over time. In facial thread lifts, PDO threads are reported to dissolve in about six months while prompting fibroblasts to produce collagen.[4] In the nose, the review describes threads as a scaffold that lifts the bridge or tip and reduces the filler volume required.[2]

The 2024 review examines adverse effects through clinical cases. Threads placed too shallowly can be visible, palpable or protrude through skin; threads along the columella can emerge inside the mouth; off-midline threads can irritate the inner nasal lining; and stretching the philtrum soon after treatment may move threads.[2]

Infection is described as rare and linked mainly to poor sterile technique, retained protruding threads or prior implants, with the nasal tip at higher risk. Dimpling is uncommon, granuloma formation is rare and mainly seen after prior nasal surgery, and tissue necrosis or blindness are described as rare complications when threads are combined with fillers.[2]

The review's prevention advice includes placing threads in the correct plane, checking the inside of the mouth after the procedure, strict aseptic technique, caution with prior implants, prompt removal of exposed threads, and limiting repeat treatments because excessive procedures can cause fibrosis.[2] For filler-based nose reshaping generally, Wikipedia identifies vascular occlusion as the most serious risk.[5]

A small registered trial of non-surgical rhinoplasty with PDO threads (n=10) was completed in 2021; results are not published in the registry entry.[3] The main published source is the 2024 case-based review, which presents individual illustrative cases rather than before-and-after measurements or patient totals.[1][2]

timeline.event: Registered pilot trial of non-surgical rhinoplasty using PDO threads starts (n=10).[3]
